title: Industrial Property Identification
name: Industrial Property Identification
metaTitle: Industrial Property Identification in Dallas, TX
metaDescription: Identifying industrial replacement property along Dallas's South Dallas and I-20 corridor for investors running a 1031 exchange on a 45-day clock.

sections.html: Industrial property has consistently been one of the more active replacement categories for Dallas 1031 exchangers, and the South Dallas and I-20 corridor in particular holds enough depth of distribution and light manufacturing stock to give a 45-day identification list a genuine set of real options to choose from. Finding the right building fast, and confirming it actually functions as an investment-grade replacement, is a different exercise than shopping for office or retail. The physical building matters as much as the location here, in a way that changes how a search actually gets run against a 45-day clock, and skipping that distinction is a common way an otherwise promising candidate turns into a problem after closing.

sections.heading: Why This Corridor Consistently Attracts Exchange Buyers
sections.html: The South Dallas industrial base along I-20 has a mix of older distribution buildings, smaller flex-industrial space, and light manufacturing product that turns over regularly enough to give an exchanger real inventory to choose from inside a tight window. Clear-height, dock door count, and trailer parking vary building to building in ways that matter more here than they would in an office search, since a tenant's operational fit depends on those specifics as much as location. A building with 24-foot clear height and ample trailer parking serves a different tenant base than a smaller flex space built for light assembly, and confusing the two during a fast search wastes time better spent on genuinely viable candidates.

sections.heading: What Real Due Diligence Looks Like on an Industrial Candidate
sections.html: Industrial buildings carry environmental due diligence risk that office and retail generally do not, prior manufacturing or fuel storage use, soil or groundwater history, underground storage tanks. A Phase I environmental assessment is standard practice before identification firms up, and on an older South Dallas building that history can take longer to trace than the 45-day window comfortably allows if it is not started early. Ordering the Phase I the moment a building becomes a serious candidate, rather than waiting until it is the clear front-runner, is the single most useful habit in this category of search. Roof condition, dock leveler function, and column spacing also get checked against what an existing or likely tenant actually needs.

sections.heading: Tenant and Lease Structure Matter as Much as the Building
sections.html: An occupied industrial replacement brings its own rent roll and lease terms into the exchange, and those need review alongside the physical building: remaining lease term, renewal options, whether the tenant is on a triple-net structure that pushes taxes and maintenance back to them, and how a single-tenant building's value depends on that tenant's ongoing occupancy. A vacant industrial building shifts the analysis toward lease-up timeline and market rent assumptions instead, which is a different risk profile for an exchanger working against a fixed identification deadline. Neither profile is automatically the wrong choice, but each demands a different set of questions before the property goes on a written identification list, and mixing up which questions apply to which type of candidate wastes time neither the exchanger nor the search can spare. A vacant building that looks like a bargain on price per square foot can turn out to be the more expensive option once realistic lease-up time and tenant improvement costs are factored into the comparison.

sections.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Candidate Goes on the Identification List
sections.html:
Before naming an industrial building in the written identification notice, the review typically covers:

  • Environmental history and whether a Phase I assessment has been completed or ordered
  • Clear height, dock door count, and trailer parking against likely tenant requirements
  • Existing lease terms, remaining term, and tenant creditworthiness if occupied
  • Roof condition, HVAC, and any deferred maintenance affecting near-term capital needs
  • Zoning and permitted use confirmation for the specific building and site

sections.heading: How This Fits Against the Rest of a Dallas Exchange Strategy
sections.html: Industrial candidates near I-20 often sit alongside suburban NNN retail or Uptown-area office options on the same identification list, since exchangers weighing asset classes want a genuine comparison rather than a single-track search. Industrial tends to offer simpler operational demands than retail once a tenant is in place, but the upfront environmental and physical due diligence has to move fast enough to clear before day 45, which is the main constraint that shapes how this search gets run.

faqs.q: How long does a Phase I environmental assessment typically take?
faqs.a: It varies by site history and consultant availability, but ordering it as soon as a building becomes a serious candidate, rather than waiting until closer to the identification deadline, gives it the best chance of completing before day 45.

faqs.q: Can a vacant industrial building still work as a 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: Yes, vacancy does not disqualify a property from being like-kind replacement real estate. It does shift the analysis toward lease-up assumptions and market rent rather than reviewing an existing rent roll, which changes the due diligence focus.

faqs.q: What makes older industrial buildings in this corridor riskier than newer product?
faqs.a: Primarily environmental history and deferred physical maintenance, prior industrial uses can leave soil or groundwater issues, and older roofs, HVAC, and dock equipment may need capital investment sooner than a newer building would.

faqs.q: Does single-tenant industrial carry different risk than multi-tenant?
faqs.a: Yes. A single-tenant building's value is more directly tied to that tenant's ongoing occupancy and creditworthiness, while a multi-tenant property spreads that risk across several leases but adds more moving parts to review during due diligence.
